summary: Redwood team walked EduNext through the Console's debugging and observability surface: request logs, distributed traces, error analysis, and the Optimize suggestions for reducing token costs. Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted, needs SOC2/compliance notes and a pilot to benchmark latency with their prompt-heavy workflows.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ben (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — alex, priya, dana from edunext, and from our side maya and carlos. we'll do a run through of the console tracing, some request logs and an example debug flow. the demo will be about 35 minutes then Q&A.

[00:00:18] Alex (EduNext): Yep sounds good. trying to figure out where we can catch perf issues in prod; our main worry is tail latency and also some weird 500 spikes last week.

[00:00:30] Maya (Redwood SE): great, i'll share my screen — sorry if the cursor is laggy — i'm in the Redwood Console, opening the Observability tab. first, request logs, you can see the per-request rows: request id, model, route, tokens in/out, latency, status.

[00:00:48] Priya (EduNext SRE): are the logs raw payloads available? we need to keep PII out but want to see prompt lengths and tokenization stats.

[00:00:55] Maya: yes, raw request logs are exportable. by default we redact PII fields if you opt in to the data protect mode; otherwise the logs show the full prompt and response body. you can also pull the logs via our API or S3 export. (slight stutter) i think i have the export pane open now.

[00:01:12] Ben: quick question on retention — what's the default retention on hosted vs dedicated?

[00:01:18] Carlos (Redwood CSM): hosted is 30 days by default, dedicated customers can configure longer retention up to 365 days if they opt into the observability add-on. for private deployments retention is customer-managed.

[00:01:30] Dana (Product PM): nice. show us the trace view you mentioned where you can see the per-token breakdown.

[00:01:36] Maya: absolutely. switching to Traces. so each trace corresponds to a request flow; if you have an orchestrated call with a few steps or tool calls you'll see subspans. here is one we pulled from the demo route — you can see the queue time, kernel execution time, kv cache hit/miss, and network egress. note the trace timestamps and the service hops — sometimes the UI will show 'model fallback' when we auto-route to a cheaper model to avoid overloading.

[00:02:10] Alex: hm when you say kv cache, is that the prefix cache? we had an issue where repeated prefixes weren't caching.

[00:02:16] Maya: yes, our 'KV cache' label is shorthand for the in-memory prefix cache and the persistent prefix store. in the trace you can click into the kv cache span and see the keys checked and the hit ratio. i can filter trace spans by 'kv_miss' to find problematic runs.

[00:02:33] Speaker 5: (unlabeled) — sorry—

[00:02:34] Priya: what about sampling? we don't want to export full traces for every request due to cost.

[00:02:37] Maya: good point — sampling policy is configurable. default is 1% for high volume routes, but you can set rule-based sampling (e.g., sample all 5xx or token>2000). we also have an on-demand trace capture — a toggle that, when enabled for a route, will capture full traces for the next N requests.

[00:02:56] Alex: that's useful. could you show an example where an error is correlated to a model fallback?

[00:03:00] Maya: sure. opening an error trace record — note the timeline: request arrives, queue latency spikes, model route returns a 429, the router automatically falls back to a smaller model, then we see a regressed quality score and the fallback span includes the 'reason: capacity' meta. the Error Analysis pane aggregates error types by route and model version.

[00:03:25] Ben: can you search by correlation id? like if our app logs include the request id, how do we jump straight to that trace?

[00:03:31] Maya: you can paste a request-id or session-id in the top search bar; we support OR queries across request id, user id, and custom tags. we also surface the link-back-to-source that you can drop into Jira or your bug tracker.

[00:03:45] Priya: on security — audit logs, RBAC. we need to know who pulled raw requests and when.

[00:03:52] Carlos: audit logs are part of the Dedicated and Private packages; they include who accessed the logs, what exports were requested, and admin actions. we also integrate with SSO/SAML for user identities and map roles to console permissions.

[00:04:05] Alex: do you support SAML attributes to map to RBAC groups? we want devs vs infra to have different permissions.

[00:04:10] Maya: yes, you can map SAML attributes to roles. we'll share our SSO config doc — i'll include the metadata file in the follow-up.

[00:04:18] Dana: okay, show the request replay or debug-run capability you mentioned earlier.

[00:04:22] Maya: right, Request Replay — pick a historical request, click 'replay', it replays against a sandbox variant of the model or against an instrumented route. you can change the model version or quantization profile and see the token-level diff and latency change. i'll demo a short replay now — switching model from rdx-3-large to rdx-3-small-quant. see latency drops by 120ms but the 'semantic drift' score increases.

[00:04:50] Alex: semantic drift score? how is that computed?

[00:04:53] Maya: it's an internal metric that compares embeddings of the original response vs replayed response and scores the divergence; we also tie to your eval prompt sets when available. it's not perfect but helps flag regressions during rollouts.

[00:05:05] Priya: what about rate limiting and throttling visibility? sometimes our app hits a burst and we see truncated responses.

[00:05:10] Maya: the console shows rate limit events per route. there's a throttle pane that breaks down requests rejected due to burst limit or concurrency cap. for Dedicated we can increase concurrency or enable burst capacity for predictable windows.

[00:05:24] Ben: (interject) for your prompt-heavy workloads, Maya, we recommended batching and prefix caching; did the Optimize suggestions section show suggestions for this account?

[00:05:31] Maya: yes, Optimize -- it scanned route telemetry and suggested a caching window for common prefixes, recommended quantized model families for certain low-stakes routes, and showed an estimated cost delta. i've got an example — here's a route with 42% repeated prefix; enabling prefix cache for 30s should reduce tokens by about 27% per our estimate.

[00:05:52] Alex: how confident are those numbers? we need real numbers against our workload.

[00:05:56] Maya: the estimates come from token-level histograms and observed hit rates; for final validation we suggest a canary rollout and A/B metrics. we can run a 1-week pilot and capture delta on tokens and latency — that's what most customers do.

[00:06:08] Priya: SLOs — can we alert on tail latency > 500ms p99?

[00:06:12] Maya: yes, alerts are configurable — p50, p90, p95, p99, error rate. alerts can be routed to PagerDuty, Slack, or email. we also support custom Webhook integrations.

[00:06:22] Alex: earlier you mentioned the ability to export traces — what format and how big are they? we worry about storage cost.

[00:06:28] Maya: you can export in JSON or OTLP (OpenTelemetry) and push to S3 or your OTel backend. size depends on sampling and whether you include raw payloads; per-trace JSONs for typical chat sessions are around 5-30 KB.

[00:06:41] Priya: can you programmatically link our internal correlation ids into Redwood traces?

[00:06:45] Maya: yes we accept custom tags on requests — x-correlation-id — and those appear as searchable fields. we recommend instrumenting the SDK to always pass your trace id.

[00:06:52] Dana: there's been mention of 'model fallback' — if that happens during peak, do you surface that as an event?

[00:06:57] Maya: we log fallback events and they show up in the Events timeline; you can alert on fallback rate so you know when routing decisions dip into lower-tier models. fallback reason metadata is included: e.g., capacity, error, or explicit policy.

[00:07:12] Alex: any demo of a real debug session where you root-caused a 500?

[00:07:15] Maya: yes i'll walk through a case. (narration) here's a spike where the service experienced a downstream BPE tokenizer error — in the trace a subspan shows tokenizer failing with exception 'bpe_invalid_byte' which caused the runtime to throw 500. i clicked the stack trace in the span and saw the model sig mismatch — customer had uploaded a slightly different tokenizer config in their private model bundle. once we corrected the tokenizer config, the errors went away.

[00:07:44] Priya: interesting — how do you surface stack traces without exposing secrets?

[00:07:48] Maya: stack traces are sanitized; we remove environment variables and file paths. in Private deployments we can provide richer debug hooks since the environment is controlled by the customer.

[00:07:58] Alex: what's the overhead of tracing — do we add 50ms to requests?

[00:08:02] Maya: minimal. sampling and the show-time trace capture has a small serialization cost (usually <5ms) and kernel timing is recorded natively on the host. heavy debug mode adds more overhead so we don't enable it by default.

[00:08:12] Ben: ok switching to some procurement notes — high-level pricing will be in the deck i'll send, but for Dedicated we have monthly reserved capacity plus an observability add-on. any compliance docs you need?

[00:08:23] Dana: SOC2 is a must. and we need to review KMS integration for key management.

[00:08:27] Carlos: we'll attach our SOC 2 and ISO docs in the follow up. KMS integration is supported for Dedicated and Private; we have an HSM option for enterprise.

[00:08:36] Alex: for the pilot, we want a config where logs are retained for 90 days and traces sampled at 5% with 100% capture for errors and 5xx. is that doable?

[00:08:44] Carlos: absolutely — that's a typical pilot profile. i'll note that in action items.

[00:08:50] Priya: one more on observability — do you provide a single pane for cross-route cost attribution? we need to show product owners cost per route.

[00:08:58] Maya: yes, the Cost Explorer breaks down token spend by route, model, and user. you can also export per-token billing level data into BigQuery.

[00:09:06] Ben: wrapping up — any open questions?

[00:09:10] Alex: timeline: if we run a 1-week pilot starting 4/21, when could we expect results and a follow-up?

[00:09:15] Carlos: results within the week of pilot, then a review session following. we'll set a follow-up the week of 4/28.

[00:09:20] Dana: please send the console recording and the trace export example.

[00:09:24] Ben: will do. thanks everyone.

[00:09:28] (end of recording)
